name: Cloud vs On-Premise
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Renting vs Owning: Where a Blockchain Node Actually Lives
lesson.summary: Businesses running blockchain nodes face the same rent-versus-own tradeoff as any other infrastructure, cloud offering flexibility and lower upfront cost against on-premise ownership offering control and lower long-run cost at scale.
lesson.body:
Once a business has accepted that running a blockchain node carries real infrastructure cost, it faces a familiar decision from the rest of enterprise computing: run that infrastructure on-premise, meaning on physical servers the company owns and houses itself, or run it in the cloud, meaning on virtual machines rented from a provider such as a major cloud computing company. This is not a blockchain-specific question in origin, businesses have made this same tradeoff for ordinary databases and web servers for years, but it takes on particular weight in a blockchain context because of exactly the infrastructure cost dynamics described in the previous section: nodes need meaningful, continuous compute, storage, and bandwidth, and a business has to decide who supplies that continuously.

On-premise infrastructure means the company buys the servers outright, a large upfront capital expense, and then bears the ongoing costs of housing them, power, cooling, physical security, and staff who can maintain and repair the hardware when it fails. In exchange, the company gets full physical control over the machines running its nodes, no reliance on a third party's uptime guarantees, and no recurring rental bill. Cloud infrastructure inverts that tradeoff: instead of a large upfront purchase, the company pays an ongoing subscription for compute and storage it does not own, which converts a capital expense into an operating expense and lets the business scale capacity up or down relatively quickly if its needs change. The cloud provider handles the physical hardware, the power, and much of the redundancy, in exchange for margin built into the price.

For most businesses experimenting with or moderately using blockchain technology, cloud infrastructure tends to win on flexibility: spinning up a new node, or several, to test a change takes minutes rather than the weeks required to procure and install physical hardware, and a company that overestimates its needs can simply scale back its cloud spending rather than owning idle servers. The tradeoff shows up over the long run and at scale, since renting indefinitely at a marked-up rate typically costs more over several years than the equivalent owned hardware would have, once the upfront purchase is amortized. A company running a small number of nodes for a pilot project has little reason to buy servers outright, while a company running large-scale, permanent, high-throughput node infrastructure has real financial incentive to consider owning at least part of it.

There is also a control dimension specific to blockchain that is easy to overlook: a node run on a major cloud provider is still, physically, running on that provider's hardware, subject to that provider's outages, that provider's regional infrastructure, and that provider's terms of service, even though the blockchain itself is decentralized. If several large blockchain projects happen to concentrate their node infrastructure on the same handful of cloud providers, a serious outage at one provider can degrade the apparent decentralization of a network that was designed specifically to avoid single points of failure. This tension between the convenience of the cloud and the risk of concentrating infrastructure with a small number of providers leads directly into the next concept: vendor lock-in, what happens when switching away from a chosen provider becomes costly enough that a business effectively cannot leave.
